paragraphs.text: A [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) cake from Yiwu, made in 2008 from leaf picked off uncultivated forest trees. Raw pu’er never gets the fast fermentation that makes ripe tea. The leaf is [fried in a wok to kill the green](sheng:making) but never hot-air dried, so some of its own activity survives, and that is what lets it go on changing for years after it is [pressed into a cake](sheng:pressing).

At eighteen years it sits between the trade's two lines. It is past the ten years that some count as [aged](sheng:ageing), and short of the twenty or more that many wait for. How far a cake has come by now depends on how tightly it was pressed and where it was kept, so its [storage](sheng:aging) is part of this tea's history.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
